Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. I'm checking the calibration figures for the 2024 propositions against the PPIC polls. For Prop 2, the late poll had it around 52%, but it finished near 57%, so the bond beat the poll by roughly five points. Prop 4's poll of 60% lined up closely with its result of 59.8%.

I'm working through the earlier propositions too: Prop 1 in 2024 eroded from a 59% poll to a 50.2% result after a late Berkeley poll. For the 2018 housing bond, a 62% yes in SurveyUSA shrank to 56.2%, which I suspect came from undecided voters breaking no.

I'm comparing the 2026 Prop 1 projection to the historical record, where late polls on bonds have sometimes overstated or understated the final yes share by several points. The chance that it drops under 50% is what I'm trying to gauge next.

I'm weighing the 2026 Prop 1 estimate: a 5–10% chance it falls under 50%, which keeps Yes clearly the likelier result, around 90–95%. The late IGS poll that showed 50% in 2024 carried 16% undecided, whereas the October PPIC poll for this year shows 60/38 with only 2% undecided, a firmer signal. I'm also noting that a November general election should draw more turnout than the low-turnout March primary of 2024, and that PPIC's likely-voter model should account for that difference.

The turnout gap matters here: a November general should draw a bigger, more Democratic electorate than the March primary, which favors Yes. The bond also has bipartisan legislative backing, and while the 2026 ballot is crowded with other measures, none of them directly bears on Prop 1. I'm also weighing the risk of voter confusion over the veterans framing, though the measure has no organized opposition beyond HJTA, Reform California, CRA, and a few newspapers.

I'm settling on Yes as the likelier winner, since a November general should bring in a larger electorate than the March primary. The question of whether the 2026 Prop 1 results are in yet is still open, though the most recent searches show nothing reported.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, so I'll search for post-election news on the bond passing or failing, using the exact dollar amount in the queries. My earlier search for results on election night turned up nothing, so this is a last check before I settle on an answer.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. I'm pulling together the bond-measure pass rates from the three sources: CalMatters puts statewide approval at about 88% since 2000, Ballotpedia at 74% since 1993, and the Treasurer's local figure for the 2026 primary is 63%. I'm now noting that the 2020 school bond, Prop 13, failed.

I'm checking how PPIC's pre-primary polling for the 2024 behavioral health bond compares with its result, since a bond at roughly 51% can still fail. I'm also weighing the 2024 school bond and climate bond polls against their results, plus some older housing bonds, to see whether late polls tend to over- or underestimate these measures.

I'm now comparing PPIC's pre-primary polling for the 2024 and older bond measures against their results, starting with the 2024 behavioral health, school, and climate bonds and then the 2020 and 2018 ones, to see whether late polls tend to over- or underestimate.

I'm comparing the late PPIC polls on the 2024 behavioral health, school, and climate bonds, and older housing and water bonds, against their actual results, which generally land close to the polling. The question is whether a 60% late-October poll for Prop 1 would hold, which seems likely given the lack of organized opposition and the funding advantage on the Yes side.

I'm weighing whether any late opposition could shift the outcome, since the No side doesn't appear to have organized committee money and the state GOP is staying neutral. Major papers like the Sacramento Bee endorsed yes, which leaves me estimating the Yes side at roughly 92 to 96 percent to win.

I'm checking whether any newspaper editorial boards came out against Prop 1, and whether the HJTA or any other group is running an organized opposition effort that could shift late voters. I'm also looking at whether any competing measure or controversy is pulling attention away from it before election day, and whether results have posted yet.

I'm now checking whether any post-election results or early returns on Prop 1 have appeared, and whether the Berkeley IGS late-October poll for the LA Times covered it, since the newsletter I saw seemed to leave it out.

I'm checking whether the IGS late-October poll covered Prop 1, and it looks like it didn't; its release only tested Prop 3 among the propositions it covered. That leaves the PPIC poll as the main public read on Prop 1, and I'm now trying to pull up the rest of PPIC's October report to confirm the 60% figure is among likely voters and was asked after the ballot label.

I'm checking the PPIC crosstabs for Prop 1 by region and party, but those breakdowns aren't essential to the answer. I'm also looking into whether the Berkeley IGS poll tested Prop 1 at all, which seems unlikely, and then moving on to how PPIC's earlier bond polls compared with their actual results.

I'm going to look up how PPIC's late polls on the 2024 school and climate bonds matched their actual results, to calibrate how far the 60% on Prop 1 might move.

content.text: PPIC's October poll is the most recent public poll on Prop 1, and the Berkeley IGS October release doesn't appear to include it. Next I'll calibrate how California bond measures have performed against late polling, since the 2020 school bond failed after polling near 51%.

I'm pulling together the polling numbers from the 2024 Prop 1 campaign: PPIC showed 68% yes in November 2023, USC/CSU/Cal Poly had 66% in January 2024, and PPIC dropped to 59% yes in February 2024. I'm now getting to the Berkeley IGS poll.

Now I'm checking the February poll against the final result: the Berkeley IGS survey showed 50% yes with 16% undecided, and the measure passed at 50.2%. That's a sharp drop from PPIC's 59% in the same month, which is a useful caution about late-stage bond polling.

I'm checking whether the 52% yes from PPIC's October 2018 survey belongs to the Prop 1 housing bond or to Prop 10, since the wording in the output doesn't line up cleanly. If it does match Prop 1, it would suggest bond measures can finish above their polling, so I want to confirm the actual PPIC October 2018 figures before relying on it.

I'm weighing the 2006 Prop 1C housing bond, which PPIC had at 57% yes in September and which I recall passing with roughly 58%. The current Prop 1 is an $11.25 billion bond with PPIC polling rising from 55% in September to 60% in October and no registered opposition campaign, unlike the 2024 measure.

I'm weighing how the current Prop 1 compares to the 2018 and 2024 Prop 1 campaigns. The 2026 measure has no registered opposition campaign, which should reduce the risk of erosion, and the electorate in a November general looks more Democratic-leaning, with Democrats more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans.

I'm checking the electorate mix against the PPIC numbers, and the weighted average of the group-level support comes out to about 60%, which matches the poll. Looking at the 2024 case, the poll had 59% in February and the result was 50.2%, so polls on this kind of measure can overstate support, though a late-October lead of 60-38 would still need a drop of more than 10 points to fail.

I'm weighing how the late-October PPIC lead of 60-38 holds up, since the 2024 Berkeley IGS poll was accurate in its final week while PPIC ran high. The 2026 measure has no Berkeley poll so far, so the only late-cycle reading is PPIC's, with just 2% undecided.

I'm now checking whether any late news about Prop 1 opposition has appeared in the final days before the election, looking for groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association or CalTax, and whether the state Republican Party has taken a position.

I'm checking whether the San Diego Union-Tribune, OC Register, or the Chronicle have endorsed for or against the housing bond, though that likely won't shift the picture much. I also want to test the 2018 Prop 1 poll figures and the 2024 bond measures against their final results to see how late polls tended to track.

I'm comparing past bond measures against their polling, noting that the 2020 school bond fell well short of its 51% reading while the 2016 school bond landed right on its poll. I'm also checking the 2024 Prop 2 and Prop 4 numbers to see how the late polls tracked their final results.

I'm now looking at Prop 2 from October 2024, where PPIC had 52% yes, and I want to check whether the measure's actual result came in well above that.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. I'm checking the calibration figures for the 2024 propositions against the PPIC polls. For Prop 2, the late poll had it around 52%, but it finished near 57%, so the bond beat the poll by roughly five points. Prop 4's poll of 60% lined up closely with its result of 59.8%.

I'm working through the earlier propositions too: Prop 1 in 2024 eroded from a 59% poll to a 50.2% result after a late Berkeley poll. For the 2018 housing bond, a 62% yes in SurveyUSA shrank to 56.2%, which I suspect came from undecided voters breaking no.

I'm comparing the 2026 Prop 1 projection to the historical record, where late polls on bonds have sometimes overstated or understated the final yes share by several points. The chance that it drops under 50% is what I'm trying to gauge next.

I'm weighing the 2026 Prop 1 estimate: a 5–10% chance it falls under 50%, which keeps Yes clearly the likelier result, around 90–95%. The late IGS poll that showed 50% in 2024 carried 16% undecided, whereas the October PPIC poll for this year shows 60/38 with only 2% undecided, a firmer signal. I'm also noting that a November general election should draw more turnout than the low-turnout March primary of 2024, and that PPIC's likely-voter model should account for that difference.

The turnout gap matters here: a November general should draw a bigger, more Democratic electorate than the March primary, which favors Yes. The bond also has bipartisan legislative backing, and while the 2026 ballot is crowded with other measures, none of them directly bears on Prop 1. I'm also weighing the risk of voter confusion over the veterans framing, though the measure has no organized opposition beyond HJTA, Reform California, CRA, and a few newspapers.

I'm settling on Yes as the likelier winner, since a November general should bring in a larger electorate than the March primary. The question of whether the 2026 Prop 1 results are in yet is still open, though the most recent searches show nothing reported.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, so I'll search for post-election news on the bond passing or failing, using the exact dollar amount in the queries. My earlier search for results on election night turned up nothing, so this is a last check before I settle on an answer.

There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.

Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

Election Results - November 3, 2026
California voters are casting their ballots for or against Proposition 40, a one-time tax on certain taxpayers with covered assets over $1 billion, with revenue primarily directed toward healthcare and portions toward food assistance or education-related programs. This page includes the latest results for Prop. 40, as well as other races in the Sacramento area.
Election Headlines

Prop. 1 would allow $11.25 billion in bonds for housing programs and veterans’ home loans. (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/elections/california-prop-1-affordable-housing-bond/103-e7aca3bf-604e-443b-be82-fefddf278b4a)

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years.
